title: Bengaluru Startup Alteon Raises $2.5 Million to Build Wind-Powered Aircraft That Can Fly for a Year
excerpt: Founded by 20-year-old Samay Sanghvi, Alteon aims to keep autonomous aircraft aloft indefinitely by harvesting energy from ocean winds — with maritime surveillance as its first use case.
body:
• Bengaluru-based Alteon raised $2.5 million in a pre-seed round led by prominent solo investor Lachy Groom, with participation from Together Fund.
  • The startup is developing small autonomous aircraft that use dynamic soaring — a technique inspired by albatrosses — to extract energy from ocean winds and stay airborne for over a year.
  • Alteon has completed more than 200 test flights in the past 30 days and recently tested autonomous flight over the Bay of Bengal at speeds exceeding 62 mph.
  • Founded by 20-year-old Samay Sanghvi, the company plans to initially deploy the aircraft for maritime surveillance.

An Aircraft That Never Lands

Prominent Silicon Valley investor Lachy Groom has backed Alteon, a Bengaluru startup attempting one of aerospace's most ambitious goals: keeping an aircraft in the sky for more than a year by harvesting energy from ocean winds.

Alteon raised $2.5 million in a pre-seed round led by Groom, with participation from Together Fund, to develop autonomous aircraft inspired by dynamic soaring — a flight technique used by albatrosses to extract energy from wind shear above the ocean. Groom committed to the investment within the first 30 minutes of meeting founder Samay Sanghvi, the 20-year-old told TechCrunch.

"Once you build airplanes that can stay in the air for more than a year, there are millions of things you can do with them."

— Samay Sanghvi, Founder, Alteon

How Dynamic Soaring Works

Conventional aircraft are fundamentally limited by the fuel or battery power they can carry. Alteon's approach aims to break that constraint entirely.

Dynamic soaring works by exploiting layers of air traveling at different speeds above the ocean's surface. The aircraft flies close to the water, climbs into faster-moving air, turns, and descends back — repeating the cycle to continuously gain energy from wind shear. The technique has been well studied in aerodynamics research but has never been demonstrated at the scale Alteon envisions.

The startup's initial design is a small, fixed-wing autonomous aircraft with a wingspan of approximately three meters. Eventually, Alteon plans to use its propellers as turbines to convert harvested wind energy into electricity, recharging onboard batteries during flight.

Early Tests Over the Bay of Bengal

Alteon has not yet demonstrated sustained energy-neutral flight — the point at which the aircraft extracts enough wind energy to remain aloft without propulsion. But the startup recently completed a key test of its autonomous flight system over the Bay of Bengal. The aircraft autonomously completed seven O-shaped cycles at speeds exceeding 62 miles per hour, flying within one meter of the water's surface, according to TechCrunch.

Dr. Gabriel Bousquet, a Silicon Valley aerospace engineer who researched dynamic soaring during his PhD at MIT, called the low-altitude ocean flight a "promising first result" but noted the harder challenge lies ahead. Reliably extracting enough energy from real-world winds means contending with turbulence, waves, spray, rain, and changing light conditions while continuously sensing a moving ocean surface.

Dr. Bharath Swaminathan, who earned his PhD from IIT Madras studying dynamic soaring stability, called the underlying physics "well established" and Alteon's effort "commendable." Even keeping an aircraft airborne for several days using this technique would itself be "a very big step, and a big achievement," he told TechCrunch.

From Hobby Models to a 20-Person Team

Sanghvi began working on what would become Alteon straight out of high school in 2023, learning to build aircraft by making — and crashing — radio-controlled models before developing early prototypes. He formally founded Alteon in 2025 and received early backing from Emergent Ventures and 1517.

The company now has a team of 20 in Bengaluru and operates from a 10,000-square-foot facility. It is building four to five aircraft per week for testing and has conducted more than 200 test flights in the past 30 days.

Maritime Surveillance First

Alteon plans to initially deploy its aircraft for maritime surveillance, giving governments real-time visibility into activity in their territorial waters. Long-endurance aerial platforms remain an unsolved problem in defense and communications — satellites are expensive, crewed aircraft costly to operate, and conventional drones limited by battery life.

Groom acknowledged the technical risk. "Ambitious problems are always going to come with risks," he told TechCrunch. "For me, it came down to believing Samay and the Alteon team are the ones to figure them out."

The next major milestone will be what Sanghvi calls "energy-neutral dynamic soaring" — proving the aircraft can fly continuously with propulsion switched off, extracting enough energy from wind alone to stay aloft.
nri_angle: Indian startup Alteon, founded by 20-year-old Samay Sanghvi in Bengaluru, secures Silicon Valley backing for ambitious autonomous aircraft technology.
